newsitem.title: USA: FOMC - What are experts looking at?.
newsitem.headline: FOMC - What are experts looking at?.

text.p: The 19-member Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) was meeting on Wednesday amid market expectations that the policy-setting arm of the Federal Reserve will leave short-term U.S. interest rates unchanged.
Following are some of the issues Fed officials -- 12 FOMC voting members, seven non-voting members -- are likely to discuss:
BEIGE BOOK:
++ The October 30 Beige Book noted "the pace of growth has slowed somewhat" and the "manufacturing sector is largely stable to stronger."
++ However, "upward pressure on wages continues to spread geographically and to grow in terms of affected occupations and range of skill levels," the Beige Book also said.
++ A Fed official told Reuters the U.S. economy is little changed from mid-September when wage pressures mounted.
++ Main argument against a Fed move today is that, one week after the U.S. presidential elections, the Fed would appear politicized and lose some credibility.
++ Another argument in favor of steady policy through year-end is the U.S. economy is in no immediate danger of overheating, removing any urgency for the Fed to move.
MONETARY POLICY GUIDES:
++ Fed sources said empirical evidence shows that, even if the non-accelerating inflation rate, or NAIRU, notion holds any truth, it is too imprecise to serve as a policy guide.
The U.S. jobless rate has been no higher than 5.8 percent -- the level some economists say fuels inflation -- since September 1994 and marked price pressures have not emerged.

++ Due to the suspected inaccuracy of output, productivity and inflation measures, there is growing support at the Fed to adopt some numerical target -- the core Consumer Price Index or the nominal Gross Domestic Product.
++ Fed officials say a numerical target would enhance the Fed's credibility and help convey intentions to the markets.
++ One Fed source told Reuters the Fed has already informally adopted that target.
FED FUNDS RATE:
++ The Fed targets the nominal federal funds rate for operating policy purposes.
++ Fed officials say the inflation-adjusted real funds rate currently is the main guideline for policy, with FOMC focusing on core CPI to estimate underlying inflation.
++ The fed funds rate has been at 5.25 percent and the discount rate at 5.0 percent since January 31, 1996. The Fed last raised the two rates on February 1, 1995.
++ According to "Taylor's rule" -- named for Stanford University economics professor John Taylor -- the funds rate is still restrictive.
However, this rule is based on the GDP deflator, and other gauges of U.S. inflation would bring the current funds rate close to neutral.
OBJECTIVES:
++ Fed officials told Reuters the central bank's main problem is to convey its intention to the markets.

++ Fed officials say markets tend not to believe the Fed is no longer running behind the inflation curve. The Fed continues to aim for price stability, "and 3.0-percent inflation is not price stability." Opportunistic disinflation -- or letting inflation fall in recessions -- is not an option, they said.
MARKET REACTION:
++ Fed officials told Reuters that potential Treasury market overreaction to Fed moves is always a concern. Fed funds futures and Eurodollars have not priced in any near-term move.
++ Traders say a surprise hike would trigger a selloff across the Treasury yield curve and crush stocks.
++ In a Reuters poll, all 37 U.S. primary dealers expect the Fed to keep the 5.25-percent federal funds rate and the 5.0-percent discount rate steady through year-end.

++ One Fed official told Reuters U.S. stocks are one source of concern because the wealth effect of the rise in stocks may give consumption a fresh boost. Also, the Fed is worried about an equity bubble. The Dow Industrials closed on Tuesday at 6266, its fifth straight record high finish.
++ One Fed source, stressing stocks have priced in a more vigorous economy than the Fed anticipates, said, "It's never a good time to prick a bubble."
++ The FOMC warned on August 20, "Policy tightening at this point might generate excessive reaction in financial markets."
GREENSPAN'S VIEWS :
++ In his last public speech on October 16, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan questioned output and productivity measures.
"Insofar as recent productivity growth is concerned, I have a serious question about the quality of the data that we employ to measure output in today's economy," Greenspan said.
On August 30 Greenspan questioned inflation measures, saying, "Is there a specific aggregate price level index for both evaluation and possible indexing on which we can rely?"

++ One source said the main argument at the Fed in favor of a 1997 slowdown is the "Greenspan rule," which holds that every sustained one-basis-point rise in long-term rates subtracts $1 billion from annual Gross Domestic Product.
Greenspan warned in July that the Fed would raise rates "should the weight of incoming evidence persuasively suggest an oncoming intensification of inflation pressures."
++ Fed officials said "persuasively" is the key word.
POLICY OUTLOOK:
++ A large majority -- 24 out of the 37 Fed watchers in the Reuters survey -- expects the next Fed move to be a rate hike.
++ Eight of 12 Fed banks requested a rate hike in late September. Several bank presidents remain inflation "hawks."
++ The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development said, "Some insurance against any re-emergence of upward trends in inflation should be bought in."
"Insurance" is seen as the key word for a 25-point move.
BIAS AND DISSENT:
++ Eight of the 37 Fed watchers saw the FOMC removing an asymmetric directive toward tightening that may have been in place since the Fed's last meeting on September 24.
++ The Fed had a tightening bias in place at its July 2-3 and August 20 meetings.
++ Policy biases have proven poor predictors of interest rate changes since 1990.
++ Dissenting FOMC votes are excellent predictors of interest rate moves. Since 1992, every dissent but one has been followed by a rate change in the same direction as the dissent.
